[["document","documents","policy","disposition","workspace","retention","administrators","Northgate"],"Understanding Retention Policies in ~8; Vault

A ~6; ~3; determines how long ~8; Vault keeps a ~1; before it becomes
eligible for permanent deletion. Every ~1; inherits exactly one ~6; ~3;, and that
~3; is resolved at the moment the ~1; is created. Changing a ~3; later affects only
~2; created after the change; it never retroactively alters the ~4; date of a
~1; that already exists. This behaviour is deliberate, because retroactive changes would
make it impossible to prove to an auditor what the ~4; schedule was at any given point
in the past.

Policies are evaluated in a fixed order. The system first looks for a ~3; attached directly to
the document. If none exists, it looks for a ~3; attached to the folder that contains the
~1;, then to that folder's parent, and so on up to the ~5; root. If no ~3; is found
anywhere on that path, the ~5; default applies. The ~5; default cannot be removed,
only changed, which guarantees that every ~1; always resolves to some policy.

There are three kinds of disposition. Soft deletion moves the ~1; to a recycle bin where it
remains visible to ~7; for a further thirty days. Hard deletion removes the ~1;
content but keeps an immutable audit stub recording that a ~1; existed, who created it, and
when it was disposed. Purge removes everything, including the audit stub, and is only available
to workspaces operating under a legal regime that requires it; most customers should never enable
purge, because it destroys the evidence that the ~6; ~3; was followed.

A legal hold suspends all ~4; for the ~2; it covers. Holds take precedence over
every ~3;, including purge, and they cannot be overridden by an administrator. Only a user with
the Legal Hold Officer role may place or release a hold, and every placement and release is
written to the audit log with the reason supplied by that user. When a hold is released, the
affected ~2; return to their normal schedule; if their ~4; date has already passed,
they become eligible immediately and will be processed in the next nightly sweep.

The nightly sweep runs at 02:00 in the ~5;'s configured timezone. It processes ~2; in
creation order, oldest first, and stops after four hours regardless of how much work remains.
Anything not processed is picked up by the next sweep. Because the sweep is time-bounded rather
than work-bounded, a ~5; with a very large backlog may take several nights to catch up, and
~7; sometimes mistake this for a failure. The sweep report, available under Reports and
Audit, shows exactly how many ~2; were considered, how many were disposed, and how many
remained in the queue when the sweep stopped.

Two questions come up repeatedly in support tickets. The first is why a ~1; with an expired
~4; date is still visible. Almost always the answer is either an active legal hold or a
backlogged sweep, both of which the sweep report will show. The second is whether a ~6;
~3; can be shortened. It can, but only for future ~2;, and the interface deliberately
makes this awkward in order to prevent an administrator from accidentally believing that existing
~2; have been reshuffled onto the shorter schedule.
"]
